We are designing bank accounts in Eventide. Your draft requirements from our
last session are in docs/design/bank-accounts/design.md. Here are my answers
to your questions.

1. Closed accounts. A closed account refuses deposits and withdrawals. An
   account can be closed only when its balance is zero, so no money is left in
   it. A closed account is never opened again.
2. A deposit that cannot be made. The money goes back into the source account,
   and the transfer fails, with the reason. The customer is told why.
3. Closing during a transfer. Yes. The bank does not stop a customer from
   closing an account because a transfer is under way.
4. Who can transfer to whom. Into any account in the bank. The source and the
   destination cannot be the same account: the app does not let the customer
   choose that.
5. Other processes. Today, only the customer's own deposits, withdrawals and
   transfers. Within the year, card payments and direct debits will take money
   out of accounts, and each month the bank will add interest and take fees.
   Statements will read each account's history.
6. Currency. Every account is in pounds sterling.

Your assumptions are all correct.

- designing-eventide-components:designing-eventide-components: Designs the commands, events, streams and handlers of Eventide components, or a change to them, before any code is written. Works from requirements to candidate models, a YAML model, and scenarios that try to break the requirements, with a human reviewer who decides. Use when asked to design an Eventide component, an event flow, or the messages of a process.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.description:

- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.

# Designing Eventide components

An event flow is the commands and events of one process, the streams they are
written to, the handlers that react to them, and the order in which one
message causes the next. This skill designs one, and checks it, before any
code is written. It produces documents, not code.

## Roles

You write the requirements in the words of the business, propose models,
write the selected model, walk scenarios through it, and find problems. The
reviewer is the person who knows the business and owns the design. The
reviewer decides:

- the words of each requirement;
- the other users of each thing that the process changes;
- the components, and the streams that each one holds;
- each problem that is accepted, and its escape hatch;
- each question in the model's `questions` and the design document's Open;
- a name, when no plain name fits a message.

This is design with the reviewer, not for the reviewer. Do not build on a
decision that the reviewer owns until the reviewer makes it. Work built on a
guess is lost when the guess is wrong, and the reviewer can then only accept
or reject it. For example, one design added a rule that its request did not
make: a closed account refuses deposits. The model, its walks and a walk by a
fresh session were built on that rule, and the two most serious problems that
they found came from it alone.

Stop and wait for the reviewer:

- when you have the draft requirements, before any candidate model;
- when you have the candidate models and their table, before you write the
  model;
- when you present the model, its scenarios and its questions;
- before you draw any panel: draw panels only when the reviewer asks;
- after the first one or two panels. The reviewer's questions on the first
  panels often change the foundations that the other panels stand on.

At each stop, write for a reviewer who has seen only what you have shown
them. Give each new or changed thing in full the first time that you show it:
a requirement in its words, a candidate in its sketch, a problem in what goes
wrong. An id alone is enough only for a thing that the reviewer has already
seen in full. A reviewer cannot judge a name: one report gave five new
requirements by their ids alone, and the reviewer could not tell whether any
of them was wrong.

## Read these first

- The feature's design document, if there is one.
- The example in `examples/purchase-orders/`: the requirements, the model and
  the scenarios of adding an assignment to a purchase order and removing it.

## The files of a design

A design is a living document. Change its files in place, and let git keep
their history; do not start a new file for a new stage or a new day. Keep a
design's files together in one folder, such as `docs/design/<topic>/`:

- `design.md`: the requirements document, the source of what the design must
  do.
- `event-flows.yaml`: the model, the source of the design.
- `scenarios.md`: the walks that test the one against the other.
- `event-flows.html`: the panels, drawn from the model.
- `changes/`: the change log.

Every correction changes the requirements, the model or the scenarios first.
If the panels and the model disagree, the model is right; fix the panels. A
date belongs in the name of a plan for one piece of work, not of a design.

The design document says what the design is now. The change log says how it
got there, and why: one file for each change, named
`YYYY-MM-DD-HHMMSS-<slug>.md` for the date and time of the decision, with a
title that carries the same date and time, and lines tagged `[decision]`,
`[rejected]`, `[finding]`, `[correction]` or `[source]`. Git records what
changed. The log records the problem, the choice, what was rejected and why,
and what it costs. A `[source]` line names the person who decided or
answered, not their role, when two people do the same job and their practice
can differ.

## Stages

Work in this order.

### 1. Requirements

Read `references/requirements-document.md`.

Before any stream, message or component, write what the process must and
must not do, in the words of the business. Define the terms first. Give each
requirement a short id. Do not say yet whether a component or the application
keeps it: the model decides that, in stage 2. The first version is a draft.
Business people often state a rule more strictly than the business needs,
because on paper the correction cost nothing and nobody saw it. The walks in
stage 3 show which rules are too strict.

Look a little into the future. For each thing whose state the process
changes, ask the reviewer which other processes change it now, and which are
likely to need it to act later. Record the answers in the design document's
"Other users". Do not design for them: they tell which components are
afferent (the rule "Afferent components take commands, and efferent
components coordinate them").

Then stop, and present the draft to the reviewer. Name each requirement that
is your assumption and not the request's. Ask only the questions whose
answers can change a stream, a component, or a requirement that a stream
rests on, such as:

- what each thing can do after it ends, such as a closed account, and what
  happens to work that is in progress when it ends;
- what the business does when a step fails after an earlier step has had an
  effect. A request often says only what happens when the first step fails;
- the other users above.

Ask each question in the words of the business, and do not say which streams
or components an answer would lead to. That is a candidate, and a candidate
shown before the answers leads the reviewer to the answer that fits it.

State each other assumption, and continue on it. Continue on an assumption
that can change the model only when the reviewer tells you to, and put its
question in Open.

### 2. Candidate models, then the model

Read `references/rules.md` and `references/model-format.md`.

- Consider more than one way to model the process with streams. They can be
  very different. A sketch is enough for a candidate: its streams, their
  keys, what each holds, and the component of each stream; for each stream,
  the commands that it takes and the events that it writes; and for each
  component, the commands that it sends and the events of other streams that
  it handles. Leave out the attributes. The messages and the handlers show the
  couplings that the row "Other users" judges.
- Decide the components in the sketches, and not before: the reviewer's
  answers to stage 1 must say what the process is first. Group the streams by
  the rule "Afferent components take commands, and efferent components
  coordinate them".
- Compare the candidates in a table. The requirements that decide where state
  lives are the rows, the candidates are the columns, and each cell says how
  that candidate keeps that requirement, in one of these words:
  - "inside one stream": one stream holds every fact that the rule needs. Its
    handler checks the rule, and accepts or rejects the command, in one write
    with `expected_version`, so nothing comes between the check and the
    result.
  - "across streams: a workflow of N steps": the facts are in more than one
    stream, so a coordinating component sends commands and handles their
    events, one step after another. Say which steps can be rejected. Between
    two steps, one is done and the next is not.
  - "a read model": the rule is checked against a read model, which can be
    out of date, so two decisions at the same time can both pass.
  - "the app only": no component checks the rule. The app checks it before it
    sends the command.

  Walk a scenario through a candidate only when the table does not decide.
- Then stop, and present to the reviewer in the conversation, in this order,
  so that nothing is compared before the reviewer has seen it:
  1. Each requirement that changed since the reviewer last saw the
     requirements, in its words, with each new assumption marked.
  2. Each candidate, the one that you recommend first: a name that says its
     idea, its sketch, and its main path walked through it with the names in
     its sketch and concrete data, such as real ids and amounts.
  3. The table, with a short label for each candidate as its column, the
     words of each requirement beside its id, and what each cell word means.
  4. The candidate that you recommend: the rows where it does better than
     the others, and the cost that you accept. A row where every candidate
     is the same decides nothing.
  5. Each candidate that you would reject: what it does better than the one
     that you recommend, and the row that rejects it. A rejection that the
     reviewer can find only in the change log is a decision that you made
     alone.

  The reviewer selects a candidate, or asks for another.
- Write the model only for the candidate that the reviewer selects, and only
  when the reviewer has agreed or corrected each assumption that can change
  it. A selection does not answer an assumption: when the reviewer selects
  and leaves one unanswered, ask again before you write the model. Record
  the choice in the design document's "Model selected". Record the
  candidates, the table, and each candidate dismissed, with why and when, in
  the change log. The selected model can look obvious afterwards; the record
  shows why it is not.
- When you write the model, move each requirement into the design document's
  Component section when the model keeps it, and into its Application section
  when only the application does.
- Before you propose a model, a rule or a name, read the change log for
  options already rejected. A rejected option comes back only when its reason
  no longer holds, and the proposal says which reason changed.
- When a decision changes a fact, or the scope narrows, search the change log
  for the decisions and rejections whose reasons rest on it, and test them
  again before you build on them. For example, a time zone on each start
  outlived its reason when the scope narrowed to one country.
- Write the whole component design in one model: every stream, message and
  handler that the requirements need. Each scenario then tests the whole
  design; do not build it from fragments that one scenario needs.

### 3. Try to break the requirements

Read `references/scenarios-format.md`.

Invent scenarios that could break a requirement, and walk each one through
the model. Start with the simplest case, and make them harder: a message
delivered twice; two requests at the same time; a second request before the
first completes; messages that arrive in a different order; a reply to a
request that was replaced; a fact that arrives after the decision that it
would have changed. Include cases that "should never happen", such as another
component that breaks its own rules. When a walk breaks only because another
component broke its own rule, name the component that owns the rule. That is
its responsibility, not a reason for a guard here.

The aim is to learn what the flow does, not to invent requirements. A walk
either holds, or it finds a problem. A problem needs a decision, which is not
always a guard. Record each problem and its decision in the design document's
"Problems found", and name it in a note on the scenario that found it. Ask,
in this order:

- **Does it leave figures that disagree after the system settles, or
  information that could mislead someone into a costly mistake?** That is not
  acceptable, however unlikely it is. A strange state with true information
  is different: "this was paid, and then it was voided" tells the operator
  what happened and what to do.
- **Can an admin put it right through the system,** with an action that the
  application offers? Or does it need a sysadmin to change data behind the
  scenes? An escape hatch often costs less than a guard.
- **How likely is it, and what does a breach cost,** against what a guard
  costs every day? Every reader, every change and every test pays for a
  guard, even if the race never comes. Greg Young offered a prize to anyone
  at his company who found a race condition in production. The prizes on the
  shelf went out of date, because nobody ever claimed one.
- Then choose: remove it by changing the design so that it cannot happen;
  guard it; detect it and correct it forward; or accept it, and name the
  escape hatch. If the choice changes what a requirement promises, change its
  words with the business, and have the reviewer agree them.

When a walk shows that a requirement needs two streams to agree, look at the
stream keys again before you add a workflow. A rule inside one stream is
cheap, because the stream orders its writes. A rule across streams or
components needs requests, replies and rejections. When no handler can keep a
requirement at the moment of its decision, because the fact arrives after
the decision, say so in a note, and say which handler reads the late fact and
what it writes, or that none does. When a walk drops a shape of the model,
add an entry to the change log, and tell the reviewer about the shape and why
it was dropped when you present the model.

**Think of it as a manual process.** Before you reach for a workflow, picture
the process done by hand, by people in a physical world, between desks and
departments. Many processes were never done by hand, and a design does not
have to copy a manual one. The picture is a way to think about races and
coordination, because in a physical world each kind of coordination has a
cost that you can see. A two-phase hold is a phone call to the other
department before every payment, and a wait for the answer. A compensating
event is asking for money back that has already left. A read of another
component's store is walking into another department to read its files.

Against those costs, the cheap answers are easy to see. A clerk pays an
invoice while another department decides to void it. The clerk acts on the
document in hand, the correction comes forward as a new document, such as an
adjustment or a credit note, that the next run picks up, and a reconciliation
finds the differences. A design can often use the same answer: a void that
arrives after a payment becomes a deduction from the next payment.

### 4. Present, only when the reviewer asks

Read `references/presenting.md`. Draw the first one or two panels, and stop
for review.

## Check the model before you present it

Read the model and the scenarios against this list, item by item:

- Every step's Caused by names an earlier step whose handler writes or sends
  its message, the operator for a command from a screen, or the component
  whose event it is.
- Every message and change in a step or a handler is declared under
  `streams` or `outside`.
- Every event and command on a stream starts with the attributes of the
  stream's key, in the key's order.
- Every scenario has a Walked line, and no handler that its steps use has
  changed since that walk.
- Every `one_of` branch and every `ignores` appears in a scenario, as a step
  whose Data names the branch or says why it is ignored, or a note or a
  comment says why not.
- Every component requirement is in the Tests of scenarios that try to break
  it, from simple to pathological. Each walk shows that the flow keeps it, or
  a problem in "Problems found" says where it does not. A permission has a
  scenario that shows it.
- Every problem in "Problems found" has a decision, and every accepted one
  names its escape hatch, or says that only a sysadmin can put it right. None
  leaves figures that disagree, or information that misleads. Every scenario
  that found a problem names it in a note.
- Every handler decides from the one entity or row that it writes, and its
  `reads` names only state of that entity or row. A scenario shows where any
  data from another component arrived.
- The handlers that write one version-gated row handle messages of one
  category.
- After the walks, no afferent component handles the events of a component
  that depends on it, or has a message, attribute or state that only one of
  its users needs. Each component, afferent or efferent, is in `questions`.
- Every handler is safe when its message arrives twice.
- The cases of stage 3 (twice, at the same time, in a different order, late)
  have a scenario, or a note says why they cannot happen.
- Comments and notes say what a reader of the model needs at that point. The
  reasoning behind a decision is in the requirements document, not repeated
  in the model.
- Every message name and attribute agrees with its source: the design
  document, or the message classes when they exist. For an `existing` stream,
  read each class that you list. An attribute that the class does not have is
  in `proposed`.
- When the design adds a state, every "latest", "last" and "current" in the
  requirements and the model is read again: the new state can make each one
  read two ways.
- Every decision and rejection whose reason rests on a fact or a scope that
  has changed is tested again.

After a large set of walks, or a change to the model, a new session walks
every scenario again against this list, from the documents alone. It is not a
continuation of the design session, and it is given no conclusions from it.
The author's own walk carries the author's assumptions, and a check that the
text agrees with the model does not check that the requirements hold. If your
agent can start a sub-agent with a fresh context, use one; if not, ask the
reviewer to start a new session. Check each finding against the documents
before you act on it, because a finding can be a misreading.

Corrections made in one pass from a walk's findings get a walk of their own,
or a check of each correction against the files, before they are committed.
Such a pass changes many places at once, and nothing else checks it: one such
pass put a wrong date in the text, and another cited a change log entry by a
guessed name. Cite a change log entry by its real file name.

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

# Bank accounts: requirements

Draft. Stage 1: requirements only. No model has been selected.

## In brief

- A customer opens an account, deposits money into it, withdraws money from
  it, and closes it.
- A withdrawal that the balance cannot cover is refused, and the customer is
  told why.
- A customer transfers money from one account to another: the money is
  withdrawn from the first account and deposited into the second.
- When the withdrawal of a transfer is refused, the transfer is cancelled and
  nothing is deposited.

## Terms

- **Customer**: a person who holds accounts.
- **Account**: a customer's store of money, with a balance in one currency.
- **Balance**: the money in an account: its deposits less its withdrawals.
- **Deposit**: money put into an account.
- **Withdrawal**: money taken out of an account.
- **Refused**: a withdrawal that has no effect on the balance, with a reason.
- **Closed account**: an account that its customer has closed.
- **Transfer**: money moved from one account (the source) to another (the
  destination), by a withdrawal from the source and a deposit into the
  destination.
- **Cancelled transfer**: a transfer whose withdrawal was refused. Nothing is
  deposited.

## Keywords

Each requirement is a **MUST** or a **MUST NOT**: something that is built and
checked. A permission is written as what the system MUST let a person do.

## Requirements

Marked *(assumption)*: not in the request.

### Accounts

- **open.** The system MUST let a customer open an account.
- **opens-empty.** *(assumption)* An account MUST open with a balance of zero.
- **close.** The system MUST let a customer close an account.

### Deposits and withdrawals

- **deposit.** The system MUST let a customer deposit money into an account.
- **withdraw.** The system MUST let a customer withdraw money from an account.
- **positive-amount.** *(assumption)* A deposit or a withdrawal MUST be of an
  amount greater than zero.
- **no-overdraft.** A withdrawal MUST be refused when it is greater than the
  balance. *(assumption)* A withdrawal of the whole balance is not refused;
  there is no overdraft.
- **refusal-reason.** When a withdrawal is refused, the customer MUST be told
  why.
- **once.** *(assumption)* Each deposit and each withdrawal MUST change the
  balance at most once, however often it is asked for.

### Transfers

- **transfer.** The system MUST let a customer transfer money from one account
  to another: the amount is withdrawn from the source and deposited into the
  destination.
- **transfer-cancelled.** When the withdrawal of a transfer is refused, the
  transfer MUST be cancelled, and nothing MUST be deposited into the
  destination.
- **transfer-reason.** *(assumption)* When a transfer is cancelled, the
  customer MUST be told why.
- **transfer-whole.** *(assumption)* When the flow settles, a transfer MUST
  have deposited exactly what it withdrew: all of it, or nothing.

## Other users

To be answered by the reviewer, for the account and its balance.

## Open

- **Q1, closed account** (close, deposit, withdraw). What can happen to an
  account after it is closed? Can money still be deposited into it, or
  withdrawn from it? Can an account be closed while it holds money, and if
  so, what happens to that money?
- **Q2, transfer into an account that cannot take it** (transfer,
  transfer-whole). If the money has left the source account, and the
  destination cannot take it, for example because it was closed in the
  meantime, what does the bank do? Return the money to the source? Hold it
  somewhere? Or can a deposit never be turned away?
- **Q3, closing during a transfer** (close, transfer). Can an account be
  closed while a transfer from it or into it is still under way?
- **Q4, who can transfer** (transfer). Can a customer transfer only between
  their own accounts, or into any customer's account? Can the source and the
  destination be the same account?
- **Q5, other users of an account** (Other users). Which other processes
  change an account's balance now, such as fees, interest, card payments or
  direct debits? Which are likely to need it later, such as statements or
  overdrafts?
- **Q6, currency** (Terms). Is every account in one currency, or can a
  transfer be between accounts in different currencies?

  balance. *(assumption)* A withdrawal of the whole balance is not refused;
  there is no overdraft.
- **refusal-reason.** When a withdrawal is refused, the customer MUST be told
  why.
- **once.** *(assumption)* Each deposit and each withdrawal MUST change the
  balance at most once, however often it is asked for.

### Transfers

- **transfer.** The system MUST let a customer transfer money from one account
  to another: the amount is withdrawn from the source and deposited into the
  destination.
- **transfer-cancelled.** When the withdrawal of a transfer is refused, the
  transfer MUST be cancelled, and nothing MUST be deposited into the
  destination.
- **transfer-reason.** *(assumption)* When a transfer is cancelled, the
  customer MUST be told why.
- **transfer-whole.** *(assumption)* When the flow settles, a transfer MUST
  have deposited exactly what it withdrew: all of it, or nothing.

## Other users

To be answered by the reviewer, for the account and its balance.

## Open

- **Q1, closed account** (close, deposit, withdraw). What can happen to an
  account after it is closed? Can money still be deposited into it, or
  withdrawn from it? Can an account be closed while it holds money, and if
  so, what happens to that money?
- **Q2, transfer into an account that cannot take it** (transfer,
  transfer-whole). If the money has left the source account, and the
  destination cannot take it, for example because it was closed in the
  meantime, what does the bank do? Return the money to the source? Hold it
  somewhere? Or can a deposit never be turned away?
- **Q3, closing during a transfer** (close, transfer). Can an account be
  closed while a transfer from it or into it is still under way?
- **Q4, who can transfer** (transfer). Can a customer transfer only between
  their own accounts, or into any customer's account? Can the source and the
  destination be the same account?
- **Q5, other users of an account** (Other users). Which other processes
  change an account's balance now, such as fees, interest, card payments or
  direct debits? Which are likely to need it later, such as statements or
  overdrafts?
- **Q6, currency** (Terms). Is every account in one currency, or can a
  transfer be between accounts in different currencies?

# The requirements document

Markdown, one living design document for each design: `design.md` in the
design's folder. The requirements are its core. Write them tersely, in the
style of an RFC, with short sentences. The requirements name no stream,
handler or message. The example is
[examples/purchase-orders/requirements.md](../examples/purchase-orders/requirements.md).

## Sections

In this order:

- **In brief.** About ten bullets: what the design does, from its streams to
  its read models, in plain words. The reviewer reads this first.
- **Background.** Only what the requirements rest on, in a few paragraphs. The
  detail of a neighbouring design, such as how a payment is calculated, goes
  in its own document in the same folder.
- **Terms.** Each word that the requirements use with a special meaning, in
  one line: "**Purchase order**: a client's order, with a value, one currency
  and one client".
- **Keywords.** Each requirement is a **MUST** or a **MUST NOT**: something
  that is built and checked. There is no SHOULD or MAY. An RFC needs them
  because independent implementations must still work together; a design has
  one implementation, so a requirement is built or it is not. A permission is
  written as what the system MUST let a person do. A requirement says only
  what the system can guarantee from what it knows: "MUST NOT pay a share
  whose void it has recorded" is a guard, and "a recovery MUST be owed" is a
  correction. When only a sysadmin can put a breach right, the requirement
  says so.
- **Requirements**, and later **Component** and **Application.** Until the
  model is written, the requirements are one section, Requirements, and name
  no component and no application: which one keeps a requirement is a
  decision of the model. When the model is written, they move into two
  sections, by where each requirement is built. The component keeps its
  requirements whoever sends the command. The application holds its screens,
  and the rules that it applies before it sends a command. Call such a rule an
  application rule, not a screen rule: its text says what the application
  MUST do. Inside each section, group the requirements by subject. Each one is
  a bold id and one or two sentences: "**settled-once.** An item MUST be
  settled at most once."
- **Out of scope.** What the process does not do, in one line each, and who
  or what does it instead.
- **Other users.** For each thing whose state the design changes, the other
  processes that change it now, and those that are likely to need it to act
  later, in one line each, as the reviewer knows them. The design does not
  build for them. They tell which components are afferent.
- **Prerequisites.** What must be in place before it goes live, in order, when
  there is any.
- **Open.** The questions that a requirement waits on, with the requirement's
  id.
- **Design coverage.** A table of the component requirements, each with the
  handler, branch or state of the selected model that keeps it. Write it when
  the model is written, before the walks: a requirement with nothing in its
  row is a gap in the design.
- **Problems found.** Each problem that a walk or a review found, by a bold
  id. Write out those that are accepted or open: what can go wrong, the escape
  hatch, and the requirement that records it. The reviewer must agree to
  them. Put those that are removed, guarded or corrected in a table, one line
  each: the id, the outcome, and the requirement that keeps it. The full story
  of each problem goes in the change log: where and when it was found, the
  answers to the questions of stage 3, and the decision.
- **Model selected.** What the model is, why it was chosen, and the costs
  accepted. Each shape that a walk or a review drops goes in the change log,
  with what it was, why, and when.

## Judging a design document

A design document is good when a reviewer can review it quickly and miss
nothing that they must decide. Judge it by these tests:

- **The first screen says what the design does.** "In brief" gives the whole
  design before any background.
- **What needs a decision is easy to find:** the requirements, the open
  questions, and the limitations accepted. None of them is only in a note, a
  table or the change log.
- **Each section serves the review.** History goes in the change log: how the
  design got here, what was dismissed, and the full story of each problem.
  The detail of another design goes in its own document. Nothing is deleted;
  it moves.
- **Each thing is said once.** A requirement is in its section, and other
  sections name its id. A reason is in the change log, and the document
  states the result.
- **Each sentence earns its place.** Ask of each one: would the reviewer miss
  it? If not, cut it or move it.
- **Plain words and short sentences**, as for the requirements.
- **Measure it.** Count the words in each section. A large section with
  nothing to decide is the first to move or to shorten. One design document
  had 7,600 words, of which 27% were resolved problems and 18% a calculation
  that the component no longer did. Moving them, and adding "In brief", cut
  it to 4,600.
# Rules

Each rule records a cost already paid or a decision already taken, with its
reason. Apply them when you sketch candidate models, when you write the
model, and when you walk the scenarios.

## Contents

- The parts of a design
- Streams, stores and state
  - A component never reads another component's store
  - Afferent components take commands, and efferent components coordinate them
  - A handler decides from the one thing that it writes
  - Reason about the entity, not about stream positions
  - An entity takes a recorded value from its event
  - A component holds its state in streams, not in an SQL database
  - A version-gated row takes updates from one category only
  - Every handler is idempotent, and the model says how
  - An entity's collections stay small for the life of its stream
- Messages
  - Name messages in plain business words
  - Say what is true now, in the words that people use
  - Name attributes within their message
  - A message carries its context
  - Give at once what is known at once
  - A command acts on the entity's current state
  - A screen action can send several commands
  - A value that is set and then changed has an Add and a Change
- Order, guards and faults
  - Accept messages in any order of arrival
  - Write from what the stream knows
  - Guard only where it is strictly necessary
  - A command's own attributes are checked by its validation
  - Stop the line on incoming data that is wrong
- Simplicity
  - Design for least surprise and solubility
  - Compensating events are a warning
  - Record every "simpler if" decision
- Keeping the documents true
  - When a term changes, change it in every current document
  - A pattern in a model is not a rule
- Patterns you will meet

## The parts of a design

- **Streams.** One stream for each entity instance. Choose the key so that
  the stream holds everything that its decisions read, and write down why.
  The command stream of a category is `<category>:command-<key>`.
- **Messages.** Commands are imperative and events are in the past tense:
  `Close` and `Closed`. When a document uses one phrase for both sides of a
  pair, such as `RefreshRequested`, give the command the imperative,
  `Refresh`, and the event a past tense. List each message's attributes, and
  mark the optional ones. Name the attribute that says who acted. A command
  for a decision that the component owns is a plain verb. A command that
  records a fact decided outside the component, such as a payment made in
  another system, starts with `Record`, because the component is not the
  authority for that fact.
- **Rejections.** A handler that refuses a command, from the entity's state,
  writes a rejection: an event that lists its reasons, so that the sender or
  the screen can react to it.
- **Domain failures.** A domain failure is an event, not an exception. When an
  action outside the store fails in a way that the business expects, such as
  an external system that refuses a stale code, the handler records it as an
  event, such as `AuthorizationFailed`, and goes on. An error of the external
  system's adapter becomes such an event. A fault of the infrastructure, such
  as a lost network or database connection, raises, and the consumer retries
  the message. A handler that raises on a domain failure stops its consumer,
  and the consumer must keep running to handle the retry that the person
  sends next. In its first test, a handler that exchanged an authorization
  code with an external system raised when the system refused a stale code,
  and its consumer stopped.
- **Handlers.** A handler reads messages, takes actions, writes messages,
  and refuses to write them. For each one, write what it reads (the message
  that it handles, and its entity), what actions it takes outside the store,
  what it writes and sends, and what it ignores. An ignore is a refusal: it
  writes nothing, and logs. A guard that nothing downstream reacts to is a
  log-and-ignore, not a rejection event. A command is ignored only when what
  it asks for is already true. One that the handler cannot do is rejected,
  because the sender waits for an answer, so no ignore applies in a state in
  which a rejection applies.

## Streams, stores and state

### A component never reads another component's store

A handler fetches only its own component's entities, and reads only its own
read models. To know something that another component owns, handle that
component's events and keep what you need in your own entity or read model.
Or send it a command and handle its reply. Within a component, each category
is projected through one store class, with one entity class.

**Why:** components are independent services with their own streams and
stores, and they communicate only through messages. A read of another
component's store couples the two, and it skips the workflow that protects the
other component's invariants.

**Why, also:** Eventide's entity cache and snapshots are not keyed by the
stream's category. The store gives the cache only the entity class and the
specifier, and the cache keeps its records by those and the id. A snapshot is
written to a stream named from the entity class's short name and the id, so an
entity class `Invoice` writes `invoice:snapshot-{id}`, whatever its component.
Two components that project the same ids into entity classes with the same
short name share that snapshot stream, and after a cache miss each restores
the other's entity data and version. Nothing fails until someone turns
snapshots on. A check that they must remember then, or a `specifier` that
they must remember to set, is not a safeguard. (Checked in evt-entity_store
2.0.4.1, evt-entity_cache 2.0.1.4 and evt-entity_snapshot-postgres 2.1.1.0.)

**In the model:** a handler decides only from the one thing that it writes
(the next rule), so no handler can read another component's store. When a
decision needs data that another component owns, a scenario must show where
that data arrived: an earlier step in which a handler of this component
received the other component's event, or a command that carries the data.

### Afferent components take commands, and efferent components coordinate them

A component's afferent couplings are the components that depend on it. Its
efferent couplings are the components that it depends on. A component depends
on another when it sends that component commands or handles its events,
because it must know that component's messages. The model shows each
coupling, in the handlers' `handles` and `sends`.

A component is afferent when many processes need to change its state. A
change to it can reach every component that depends on it, so it is hard to
change. Keep change in it to a minimum. It takes commands: each process that
needs it sends it commands and handles its events, so a new process needs no
change in it. It does not handle the events of the components that depend on
it. It holds no message, attribute or state that only one of its users needs,
such as an attribute that every other sender leaves empty.

A component is efferent when it depends on many components, and few or none
depend on it. It costs little to change. It tends to be a coordinating
component: it sends commands to afferent components and handles their events.
Put a process, and the state and guards that it needs, in an efferent
component, where change is cheap.

Which components are afferent is a fact of the business: how many processes
change a thing, now and later. One design's requirements often name only one
of them.

**Why:** a design put the transfer of money between two accounts in the
account stream, with no stream for the transfer. The account then had
transfer commands and events, a list of its transfers in progress, a
transfer's id on its deposit that every other deposit left empty, and a guard
so that a deposit from another sender could not end a transfer. Every other
process that moves money in or out of an account would add the same to the
account.

**In the model:** after the walks, read the couplings again, and put each
component, afferent or efferent, to the reviewer in `questions`, with the
couplings that support it.

### A handler decides from the one thing that it writes

A handler that writes events decides from one entity: the entity of the stream
that it writes, fetched with its version. A handler that upserts a read-model
row decides from that row. It reads nothing else to decide: no second entity,
and no read model. Data that the decision needs from elsewhere comes in the
message. A command carries what the screen read from a read model, and an
event handler keeps what it needs in its own entity.

**Why:** the write with `expected_version` orders the decision against every
other write to that stream. A second stream or a read model has its own order,
and nothing ties it to the write, so a decision that reads it can act on an
old view without knowing. For example, a payment handler that read a read
model to find voided documents could act on a list that had not caught up.
Instead, the command carries the amounts of the documents that the person
saw, and a void that arrives after the payment is corrected in a later
payment.

It also keeps a reader and the stream that it reads in one component. A
handler that only reads a second stream of its own component still works when
that stream is later moved into a component of its own, and it then reads
another component's store, which the previous rule forbids. A handler that
writes the stream that it decides from cannot be separated from it.

**In the model:** `reads` lists the state of that one entity or row that the
decision uses: `reads: [pending_addition_id]`. A handler that decides nothing
has no `reads`.

### Reason about the entity, not about stream positions

A handler fetches its entity as projected from the whole stream up to its
head, not up to the message that it is handling. The message is a trigger to
act. The state comes from the entity, and the entity is a record of decisions
already taken. So in a scenario walk, ask "what does the entity look like when
the handler fetches it?", not "what has the consumer seen at this position?".
Across components, ask what has arrived in your own entity or read model. That
can lag.

**Why:** a handler wrote a "complete" event when the last of three expected
documents arrived. Its consumer was stopped while all three arrivals were
written. When it started again, it handled each arrival against the entity
projected to the head of the stream, found all three documents each time, and
wrote "complete" three times. The design had assumed that only the handler of
the third arrival would see three.

### An entity takes a recorded value from its event

When an event records a value that a handler calculated, such as a total, the
projection takes the value from that event. It does not calculate it again
from other values in the stream. A projection calculates only a value that no
event records, and only until an event records it.

**Why:** the recorded value is the fact, and a second calculation can give
another result. In one design, a document's entity calculated its totals from
its lines, and did not apply the totals that its issued event recorded. For
documents whose lines were in an older event that the projection no longer
applied, the entity had totals of zero, while the issued event held the
correct totals. A void that copied the document's details from the entity
would have recorded the zeros.

**In the model:** when a handler `reads` a value that an event records, the
stream's comment names that event. For a value that no event records, the
comment says what the entity calculates it from.

### A component holds its state in streams, not in an SQL database

A component's handlers write events to the component's own streams. They do
not, as a matter of course, write what they handle into a database table. An
SQL database exists to answer queries, and a component's handlers do not
query. They fetch one entity from one stream.

There are two uses for a database, and both are queries:

- **The read side.** Screens query, so a read model is built for them, by
  consumers of the component's events. It is fed from the streams, not
  instead of them. The application that owns the screens can own the read
  model too, so a screen is not by itself a reason for the component to have
  a database.
- **A genuine query across streams.** The message store reads one stream at a
  time. When a decision needs data from two structures that cannot share a
  stream, a database is the only way: for example, items published on one
  side, and the people who subscribe to their categories on the other. That
  need is rare, and a design should try to avoid it.

**Why:** a draft model had a consumer upsert rows instead of writing events.
The design then had no stream that recorded the arrival of the upstream fact,
and nothing in the component could react to it.

**In the model:** a consumer of another component's event writes that event
to a stream of this component, under the event's name with its stream's name
in front: `invoice.Issued` becomes `InvoiceIssued`. It is a plain copy: the
attributes of the stream's key first, then every attribute of the upstream
event. The consumer chooses only the streams. It does not choose parts of the
event or calculate, so that its one job stays simple; anything that follows is
a handler of the copy. An `outside` read model is written only by handlers of
this component's own events, or it is a genuine query across streams, with a
note that says why.

### A version-gated row takes updates from one category only

A read-model row whose version is the global position of the message that
last wrote it ignores a message whose position is not newer. Messages of one
category reach their consumer in the order of their positions, but messages
of two categories do not. So when two consumers update the same row, an
update that arrives late carries a lower position than one already applied,
and it is lost without an error.

**Why:** a draft model had a second consumer write a flag onto a row that the
first consumer also updates. A correction that arrived after the flag would
have been dropped.

**In the model:** the handlers that write one row handle messages of one
category. When another category must add to that row, give it a row of its
own.

### Every handler is idempotent, and the model says how

Messages are delivered at least once. A handler cannot tell from its stream
position that it did the work before ("Reason about the entity"), so its
idempotence must be explicit. These are the mechanisms.

- **A sequence check**, the usual default. The entity records, for each
  source, the global position of the last message that it applied. The
  handler first checks the message's position against it, and logs and
  ignores a message that it has already processed. This works only while the
  positions of the messages that cause the events in a stream never go down:
  an event that follows an older message lowers the recorded position, and
  messages already handled are then handled again. It is also not safe for a
  consumer that may be replayed from an earlier position to pick up what it
  skipped, when the position is kept for each source category: the skipped
  message is now below the recorded position, and it is ignored as
  processed. Such a consumer keeps the position for each source stream.
- **A reservation.** This is for a command that carries its own idempotence
  key. The handler first writes a copy of the command, with `write.initial`,
  to a stream keyed by the original ids plus the key. A second copy finds
  that stream and is ignored. The handler's block runs each time it handles
  the copy, as on a consumer replay, so the block still starts with the
  sequence check. A command takes the reservation when it can be sent again
  out of order and sets a state that another command can reverse, such as a
  start that can be cancelled, or terms that can change back. Once the state
  has come back, a check of the entity cannot tell a copy from a new command;
  only the id can. A command whose state never comes back, such as the
  closing of something that cannot reopen, is ignored by state and needs no
  id.
- **A version-gated upsert.** A read-model row written with the message's
  global position as its version ignores a version that is older or equal.
- **Ids that stay the same on a retry:** an id that the client supplies, or
  a deterministic UUID v5 of the ids that make the request unique.
- **A state guard.** A transition that is already done, such as a second
  set-up, is logged and ignored.

Optimistic concurrency is not idempotence, but it goes with it. The handler
fetches with `include: :version` and writes with `expected_version`. On a
conflict the consumer retries the message: it fetches again and decides
again. Fetch, decide, write and retry are one unit.

**Why:** a notification handler recorded nothing about the documents that it
had notified. Only its consumer's position kept it away from them. When the
handler moved to a consumer with a new position, that consumer read the
category from the start and sent the notifications for every old document
again.

**In the model:** a handler that does not use the sequence check says which
mechanism it uses, in `idempotence`.

### An entity's collections stay small for the life of its stream

A consumer keeps each entity that it fetches in memory, whole, for as long as
it runs: Eventide's entity cache keeps the entities in a hash, and nothing
takes one out. So a consumer's memory is the number of entities that it has
handled times their size. A collection on an entity, such as a list of start
dates or a set of the documents that it has recorded, grows each time a
message adds an entry. When the stream lives for years and the entries come
with volume, the entity grows for years.

Before an entity keeps a collection, know three things: what one entry holds,
what adds an entry and how often, and how long the stream lives.

- Entries that come with a rare business act are safe. An agreement that
  keeps each of its starts, with the end date of each, gains one entry each
  time it starts again, a few times in its life. Such a collection can be the
  smallest correct state: when the latest start can be cancelled and the one
  before it then applies again, the entity cannot keep only the latest two.
- Entries that come with volume are not safe: one for each invoice, payment
  or source stream, on a stream that lives as long as the company. Keep only
  the entries that a decision still reads, and drop each one when no decision
  can read it again; or keep a total in place of the entries; or split the
  stream by period, so that each stream ends.
- A sequence kept for each source stream, for idempotence ("Every handler is
  idempotent"), is such a collection.

**Why:** an entity that grows shows no fault in the tests or at go-live. Its
cost shows years later, as a consumer whose memory grows until it is stopped.
Snapshots make a fetch shorter, but the entity in memory is the same size.

**In the model:** a handler's `reads` names what the entity keeps. For each
collection in it, the stream's comment says what adds an entry, how often,
and what keeps the collection small.

## Messages

### Name messages in plain business words

Command and event names avoid technical words, so that someone who knows the
business can read a stream and understand it. It is not always possible, but
it is the aim. A command named `VoidAgreementEnd` was correct, but nobody in
the business would say it. `Reopen` then read as opening something again,
once the design had another thing that opens and closes. `RemoveEndDate`, the
words that its screen shows, fitted. A plain word can still mislead when the
same design uses it for something else. A command's name is also the label
that the screen shows for it: if the screen would not show it, it is the
wrong name.

When no name fits at all, the problem is usually in the design, not in the
words: the message is not clear about what it does or, more often, it
combines two or more things that should be separate. For example, an event
that both moved an entity's start time earlier and said that the messages
missed since then must be replayed had no name that fitted, because it
combined a fact about the entity with an operation. Apart, the fact had a
plain name, and the replay needed no message at all.

An event about the whole entity is a bare verb, and an event about a part of
it names the part. A purchase order is `Created`, `Closed` and `Reopened`,
but has an `EndDateAdded`; an invoice is `Issued` and `Voided`, but has a
`DueDateCorrected`. The command follows its event: `Close`, but
`AddEndDate`. Before you drop the entity's name, check that the event is
about the whole entity. A command that cancels only the latest start of an
agreement cancels a part of it, so its event is `StartCancelled`: a bare
`Cancelled` would say that the whole agreement was cancelled. Its screen can
still say "Cancel agreement": this rule wins over the rule that a command's
name is its screen label, because a reader of the stream must see that only a
start was cancelled.

**In the model:** read each command and event name aloud, as the operator
would say it. If it needs explaining, look for the word that the business
uses. If no plain word fits, keep the name, and say why in a comment. If no
name fits at all, look at the design first: separate what the message
combines, or make clear what it does. When one round of names fails, do not
offer another. Say that no name fits, and ask what the message combines.

### Say what is true now, in the words that people use

A design reads its streams as records, and its words drift into the words of
records: "a start", "an end", "the agreement has a start that is not
cancelled". Then a word such as *started* has two meanings: that the stream
holds a `Started` event, and that the thing is running now. People use it only
in the second meaning. An engine that was started and then turned off is not
started, and nobody refuses to start it because it is "already started". So an
agreement that has ended is not started.

- A word for a state, such as started, ended, in force, open or closed, means
  the state now.
- A rule that depends on history says so, with words for history: "has been
  started", "was in force on 3 Oct", "has never started".
- A refusal reason says what stands in the way, as you would say it to the
  person who sent the command: `already_started`, `already_ended`,
  `not_after_last_end_date`. A negation is correct when it is what a person
  says. A reason is not the model's condition made shorter: one design's
  refusal `not_ended` was "the latest active start has no end" made shorter,
  and it became `already_started`.
- The `when` conditions use the same words, because the reasons, the code and
  the screens are written from them.

**Why:** a word with two meanings makes each reader choose one. The code, the
screens and the messages that a person sees are then written from different
meanings, and nobody notices until a reader asks what the word means.

**In the model:** read each condition, ignore and reason aloud, as you would
say it to the operator about the thing now. Where a word for a state means
"the stream holds this event", say the state, or mark the history.

### Name attributes within their message

An attribute is named within the scope of its message. The message's name
says what the fact is, so the attribute does not repeat it: an `Opened` event
has `time`, the time from which the thing is open, not `open_time`, and a
`PaymentTimeCorrected` has `time` for the corrected payment time. An id keeps
the name of the entity that it identifies, such as `invoice_id`, never a bare
`id`.

`time` is the time of the message's own fact, and an event copies it from its
command. Most commands do not need it. A command carries `time` when the
fact's time differs from the time at which it is processed and a consumer of
the event needs it: an import of history written today for actions taken
months ago, or an effective date that a back office enters later. Say why in
a comment on the command. `processed_time` is the time at which the handler
wrote the event, from the
clock, and an event carries it only when the business needs to know it.
Message DB records when it wrote each message in any case.

**Why:** a void event carried a bare `date`, copied from the event that made
the charge. Later, nobody could tell if it was the date of the charge or the
date from which the void applied. In the same way, three components set `time`
t

6	handler or message. The example is

8	
9	## Sections
10	
11	In this order:
12	
13	- **In brief.** About ten bullets: what the design does, from its streams to
14	  its read models, in plain words. The reviewer reads this first.
15	- **Background.** Only what the requirements rest on, in a few paragraphs. The
16	  detail of a neighbouring design, such as how a payment is calculated, goes
17	  in its own document in the same folder.
18	- **Terms.** Each word that the requirements use with a special meaning, in
19	  one line: "**Purchase order**: a client's order, with a value, one currency
20	  and one client".
21	- **Keywords.** Each requirement is a **MUST** or a **MUST NOT**: something
22	  that is built and checked. There is no SHOULD or MAY. An RFC needs them
23	  because independent implementations must still work together; a design has
24	  one implementation, so a requirement is built or it is not. A permission is
25	  written as what the system MUST let a person do. A requirement says only
26	  what the system can guarantee from what it knows: "MUST NOT pay a share
27	  whose void it has recorded" is a guard, and "a recovery MUST be owed" is a
28	  correction. When only a sysadmin can put a breach right, the requirement
29	  says so.
30	- **Requirements**, and later **Component** and **Application.** Until the
31	  model is written, the requirements are one section, Requirements, and name
32	  no component and no application: which one keeps a requirement is a
33	  decision of the model. When the model is written, they move into two
34	  sections, by where each requirement is built. The component keeps its
35	  requirements whoever sends the command. The application holds its screens,
36	  and the rules that it applies before it sends a command. Call such a rule an
37	  application rule, not a screen rule: its text says what the application
38	  MUST do. Inside each section, group the requirements by subject. Each one is
39	  a bold id and one or two sentences: "**settled-once.** An item MUST be
40	  settled at most once."
41	- **Out of scope.** What the process does not do, in one line each, and who
42	  or what does it instead.
43	- **Other users.** For each thing whose state the design changes, the other
44	  processes that change it now, and those that are likely to need it to act
45	  later, in one line each, as the reviewer knows them. The design does not
46	  build for them. They tell which components are afferent.
47	- **Prerequisites.** What must be in place before it goes live, in order, when
48	  there is any.
49	- **Open.** The questions that a requirement waits on, with the requirement's
50	  id.
51	- **Design coverage.** A table of the component requirements, each with the
52	  handler, branch or state of the selected model that keeps it. Write it when
53	  the model is written, before the walks: a requirement with nothing in its
54	  row is a gap in the design.
55	- **Problems found.** Each problem that a walk or a review found, by a bold
56	  id. Write out those that are accepted or open: what can go wrong, the escape
57	  hatch, and the requirement that records it. The reviewer must agree to
58	  them. Put those that are removed, guarded or corrected in a table, one line
59	  each: the id, the outcome, and the requirement that keeps it. The full story
60	  of each problem goes in the change log: where and when it was found, the
61	  answers to the questions of stage 3, and the decision.
62	- **Model selected.** What the model is, why it was chosen, and the costs
63	  accepted. Each shape that a walk or a review drops goes in the change log,
64	  with what it was, why, and when.
65	
66	## Judging a design document
67	
68	A design document is good when a reviewer can review it quickly and miss
69	nothing that they must decide. Judge it by these tests:
70	
71	- **The first screen says what the design does.** "In brief" gives the whole
72	  design before any background.
73	- **What needs a decision is easy to find:** the requirements, the open
74	  questions, and the limitations accepted. None of them is only in a note, a
75	  table or the change log.
76	- **Each section serves the review.** History goes in the change log: how the
77	  design got here, what was dismissed, and the full story of each problem.
78	  The detail of another design goes in its own document. Nothing is deleted;
79	  it moves.
80	- **Each thing is said once.** A requirement is in its section, and other
81	  sections name its id. A reason is in the change log, and the document
82	  states the result.
83	- **Each sentence earns its place.** Ask of each one: would the reviewer miss
84	  it? If not, cut it or move it.
85	- **Plain words and short sentences**, as for the requirements.
86	- **Measure it.** Count the words in each section. A large section with
87	  nothing to decide is the first to move or to shorten. One design document

design's folder. The requirements are its core. Write them tersely, in the
style of an RFC, with short sentences. The requirements name no stream,
handler or message. The example is
[examples/purchase-orders/requirements.md](../examples/purchase-orders/requirements.md).

## Sections

In this order:

- **In brief.** About ten bullets: what the design does, from its streams to
  its read models, in plain words. The reviewer reads this first.
- **Background.** Only what the requirements rest on, in a few paragraphs. The
  detail of a neighbouring design, such as how a payment is calculated, goes
  in its own document in the same folder.
- **Terms.** Each word that the requirements use with a special meaning, in
  one line: "**Purchase order**: a client's order, with a value, one currency
  and one client".
- **Keywords.** Each requirement is a **MUST** or a **MUST NOT**: something
  that is built and checked. There is no SHOULD or MAY. An RFC needs them
  because independent implementations must still work together; a design has
  one implementation, so a requirement is built or it is not. A permission is
  written as what the system MUST let a person do. A requirement says only
  what the system can guarantee from what it knows: "MUST NOT pay a share
  whose void it has recorded" is a guard, and "a recovery MUST be owed" is a
  correction. When only a sysadmin can put a breach right, the requirement
  says so.
- **Requirements**, and later **Component** and **Application.** Until the
  model is written, the requirements are one section, Requirements, and name
  no component and no application: which one keeps a requirement is a
  decision of the model. When the model is written, they move into two
  sections, by where each requirement is built. The component keeps its
  requirements whoever sends the command. The application holds its screens,
  and the rules that it applies before it sends a command. Call such a rule an
  application rule, not a screen rule: its text says what the application
  MUST do. Inside each section, group the requirements by subject. Each one is
  a bold id and one or two sentences: "**settled-once.** An item MUST be
  settled at most once."
- **Out of scope.** What the process does not do, in one line each, and who
  or what does it instead.
- **Other users.** For each thing whose state the design changes, the other
  processes that change it now, and those that are likely to need it to act
  later, in one line each, as the reviewer knows them. The design does not
  build for them. They tell which components are afferent.
- **Prerequisites.** What must be in place before it goes live, in order, when
  there is any.
- **Open.** The questions that a requirement waits on, with the requirement's
  id.
- **Design coverage.** A table of the component requirements, each with the
  handler, branch or state of the selected model that keeps it. Write it when
  the model is written, before the walks: a requirement with nothing in its
  row is a gap in the design.
- **Problems found.** Each problem that a walk or a review found, by a bold
  id. Write out those that are accepted or open: what can go wrong, the escape
  hatch, and the requirement that records it. The reviewer must agree to
  them. Put those that are removed, guarded or corrected in a table, one line

  accepted. Each shape that a walk or a review drops goes in the change log,
  with what it was, why, and when.

A design document is good when a reviewer can review it quickly and miss
nothing that they must decide. Judge it by these tests:

- **The first screen says what the design does.** "In brief" gives the whole
  design before any background.
- **What needs a decision is easy to find:** the requirements, the open
  questions, and the limitations accepted. None of them is only in a note, a
  table or the change log.
